column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 28: “Hold to my Sunnah”

column2: From al-ʿIrbāḍ ibn Sāriyah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ admonished us with an admonition at which the hearts trembled and the eyes shed tears. We said: Messenger of Allah, it is as though it were the admonition of one bidding farewell, so give us your counsel. He said: “I counsel you to fear Allah, and to listen and obey,

even if a slave is put in command over you. Whoever of you lives after me will see much disagreement. So hold to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided (rāshidūn), guided (mahdiyyūn) caliphs; bite onto it with your molar teeth. And beware of newly invented matters, for every innovation is misguidance.” Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī reported it, and al-Tirmidhī said: A ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ hadith.
This hadith was recorded by Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah through the narration of Thawr ibn Yazīd, from Khālid ibn Maʿdān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr al-Sulamī.
Aḥmad, in one of his narrations, and Abū Dāwūd added: and Ḥujr ibn Ḥujr al-Kalāʿī, both of them from al-ʿIrbāḍ ibn Sāriyah. Al-Tirmidhī said: Ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. The ḥāfiẓ Abū Nuʿaym said:
It is a sound hadith, among the authentic hadiths of the people of al-Shām. He said: Al-Bukhārī and Muslim did not leave it out because they found anything objectionable in it.

Al-Ḥākim claimed that the reason they left it out was that they imagined it had no narrator from Khālid ibn Maʿdān other than Thawr ibn Yazīd; yet Baḥīr ibn Saʿd, Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Taymī and others also narrated it from him.

I say: The matter is not as he supposed, and the hadith does not meet their conditions. They recorded nothing at all from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr al-Sulamī or from Ḥujr al-Kalāʿī, and neither of these is among those famous for knowledge and narration.
Moreover, it has been reported from Khālid ibn Maʿdān in differing ways. Some narrate it from him as given above; others narrate it from him, from Ibn Abī Bilāl, from al-ʿIrbāḍ,
Imam Aḥmad recorded it by this route as well. It has also been narrated from Ḍamrah ibn Ḥabīb, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr al-Sulamī,

from al-ʿIrbāḍ; Imam Aḥmad and Ibn Mājah recorded it by his route. In his version Ḍamrah added: “I have left you upon the shining white [path], whose night is like its day; none swerves from it after me but one who is doomed.” And at the end of the hadith he added: “For the believer is like the camel with a sore nose: wherever it is led, it follows.”
A group of the ḥuffāẓ rejected this addition at the end of the hadith, saying that it was interpolated (mudraj) into it and was not part of it. Aḥmad ibn Ṣāliḥ al-Miṣrī and others said this.
Al-Ḥākim recorded it and said in his version: Asad ibn Wadāʿah used to add to this hadith: “For the believer is like the camel with a sore nose: wherever it is led, it follows.”

Ibn Mājah also recorded it through the narration of ʿAbdullāh ibn al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Zabr: Yaḥyā ibn Abī al-Muṭāʿ told me: I heard al-ʿIrbāḍ — and he related it. On the face of it, this is a sound, connected chain whose narrators are well-known and trustworthy,

and hearing is stated explicitly in it. Relying on this narration, al-Bukhārī mentioned in his Tārīkh that Yaḥyā ibn Abī al-Muṭāʿ heard from al-ʿIrbāḍ. But the ḥuffāẓ of al-Shām rejected that, saying:

Yaḥyā ibn Abī al-Muṭāʿ did not hear from al-ʿIrbāḍ and never met him, and this narration is a mistake. Among those who said so was Abū Zurʿah al-Dimashqī, who related it from Duḥaym; and these men know their own shaykhs better than others do.

Al-Bukhārī (may Allah have mercy on him) fell into errors in his Tārīkh over reports about the people of al-Shām. The hadith has been narrated from al-ʿIrbāḍ by other routes, and it has also been narrated from the hadith of Buraydah, from the Prophet ﷺ; but the chain of Buraydah's hadith is not established. And Allah knows best.

Al-ʿIrbāḍ's words, “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ admonished us with an admonition”: in the narration of Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī, “an eloquent one”, and in their narration this was after the dawn prayer.

The Prophet ﷺ often admonished his Companions outside the regular sermons, such as the sermons of Fridays and the Eids. Allah the Exalted had commanded him to do so, saying: “Admonish them, and speak to them about themselves with eloquent words” [al-Nisāʾ 4:63]; and: “Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition” [al-Naḥl 16:125].

But he did not admonish them constantly; rather, he gave it to them at intervals, as in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Wāʾil, who said: ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd used to remind us every Thursday, and a man said to him: Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān,

we love your talk and long for it, and we wish you would speak to us every day. He said: Nothing keeps me from speaking to you except dislike of wearying you. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to give us admonition at intervals, disliking that we should grow weary.
Eloquence in admonition is commendable,

because it is more likely to win the hearts' acceptance and draw them in. Eloquence is to succeed in making the intended meanings understood, and in conveying them to the hearts of the listeners in the finest form of words that express them, the most correct of them, the sweetest to the ear and the most effective on the heart.
He ﷺ used to keep his sermons short and not lengthen them; rather, he was eloquent and concise.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Jābir ibn Samurah, who said: I used to pray with the Prophet ﷺ, and his prayer was moderate and his sermon was moderate.
Abū Dāwūd recorded it, and his wording is: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not make the admonition long on Friday; it was only a few brief words.
Muslim recorded, from the hadith of Abū Wāʾil, who said:
ʿAmmār preached to us, concisely and eloquently. When he came down, we said: Abū al-Yaqẓān, you were eloquent and concise; if only you had taken a little longer! He said:
I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “A man's long prayer and short sermon are a sign of his understanding; so make the prayer long and the sermon short, for some eloquence is magic.”
Imam Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of al-Ḥakam ibn Ḥazn, who said:
I attended the Friday prayer with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He stood leaning on a staff or a bow, and praised Allah and extolled Him with a few light, good and blessed words.

Abū Dāwūd recorded, from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, that a man stood up one day and spoke at length, and ʿAmr said: Had he been moderate in his speech, it would have been better for him. I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:
“I have seen fit” — or “I have been commanded” — “to be brief in speech, for brevity is better.”

His words, “the eyes shed tears and the hearts trembled”: these are the two qualities for which Allah praised the believers on hearing His remembrance, as the Exalted says: “The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned” [al-Anfāl 8:2];

and He says: “And give good tidings to the humble, whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned” [al-Ḥajj 22:34–35]; and He says: “Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves at the remembrance of Allah and the truth that has come down?” [al-Ḥadīd 57:16];

and He says: “Allah has sent down the best of speech, a Book consistent and oft-repeated, at which the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah” [al-Zumar 39:23]; and the Exalted says: “When they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they recognise” [al-Māʾidah 5:83].

His state ﷺ would change when he admonished, as Jābir said: When the Prophet ﷺ preached and mentioned the Hour, his anger grew intense, his voice rose and his eyes reddened, as though he were warning of an army and saying: It will fall on you in the morning! It will fall on you in the evening!
Muslim recorded it in this sense.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Anas: The Prophet ﷺ came out when the sun had passed its zenith and prayed ẓuhr, and when he had said the closing salām,
he stood on the pulpit and mentioned the Hour, and mentioned that before it there would be momentous events. Then he said: “Whoever would like to ask about anything, let him ask about it;
for by Allah, you will not ask me about anything but I will tell you of it while I stand here.” Anas said: The people wept a great deal,
and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept saying: “Ask me.” A man stood up and said: Where shall I enter, Messenger of Allah? He said: “The Fire.” And he related the rest of the hadith.
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr: He gave a sermon and said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ preaching and saying:

“I have warned you of the Fire! I have warned you of the Fire!” — so loudly that a man in the market would have heard him from where I am standing now. He said: until a striped cloak that was on his shoulder fell down at his feet.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Guard yourselves against the Fire.” He said: And he turned his face aside. Then he said:

“Guard yourselves against the Fire,” and turned away and averted his face three times, until we thought he was looking at it. Then he said: “Guard yourselves against the Fire, even with half a date; and whoever cannot find that, then with a good word.”
Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn Salimah, from ʿAlī or from al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to preach to us

and remind us of the Days of Allah, until it could be seen in his face, as though he were the warner of a people whom the thing would strike at dawn. When he had just been with Jibrīl, he would not smile or laugh until it had lifted from him.
Al-Ṭabarānī and al-Bazzār recorded it from the hadith of Jābir, who said: When revelation came to the Prophet ﷺ, or when he admonished, I would say:

[He is] the warner of a people upon whom the punishment has come. Then, when that had left him, I would see him the most cheerful of people in countenance, the most given to laughter and the brightest of them in expression ﷺ.

Their words, “Messenger of Allah, it is as though it were the admonition of one bidding farewell, so give us your counsel,” show that in that admonition he ﷺ had gone further in eloquence than in others;

that is why they understood it to be the admonition of one bidding farewell, for one who is bidding farewell is more thorough in word and deed than anyone else. For that reason the Prophet ﷺ commanded that one pray the prayer of one bidding farewell,
because whoever senses that he is bidding farewell with his prayer perfects it in the most complete way.

Perhaps he ﷺ had also hinted at a farewell in that sermon, as he hinted at it in his sermon at the Farewell Ḥajj, where he said: “I do not know; perhaps I will not meet you after this year of mine,” and began bidding people farewell, so that they said: This is the Farewell Ḥajj.
When he returned from his Ḥajj to Madīnah, he gathered the people at a watering place between Makkah and Madīnah called Khumm, and preached to them, saying: “O people,

I am only a human being; soon the messenger of my Lord may come to me and I will answer.” Then he urged them to hold fast to the Book of Allah, and enjoined them to care for the people of his household. Muslim recorded it.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs — the wording being Muslim's — from ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed over those killed at Uḥud, and then went up onto the pulpit like one bidding farewell to the living and the dead, and said:

“I shall go ahead of you to the Pool, and its breadth is like the distance from Aylah to al-Juḥfah. I do not fear that you will associate partners with Allah after me; but I fear for you this world, that you will compete for it and fight one another and perish, as those before you perished.”
ʿUqbah said: It was the last time I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the pulpit.
Imam Aḥmad recorded it with the wording: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed over those killed at Uḥud after eight years, like one bidding farewell to the living and the dead;

then he went up onto the pulpit and said: “I shall go ahead of you, and I am a witness over you. Your meeting place is the Pool, and I am looking at it now. I do not fear disbelief for you, but this world: that you will compete for it.”

Imam Aḥmad also recorded, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came out to us one day like one bidding farewell and said: “I am Muḥammad, the unlettered Prophet” — saying it three times — “and there is no prophet after me.

I have been given the openings of speech, its conclusions and its comprehensive forms. I have been taught how many are the keepers of the Fire and the bearers of the Throne. My Lord has dealt leniently with me, I have been granted well-being, and my nation has been pardoned. So listen and obey as long as I am among you; and when I am taken away, hold to the Book of Allah: treat as lawful what it makes lawful, and treat as unlawful what it makes unlawful.”
Perhaps the sermon to which al-ʿIrbāḍ ibn Sāriyah referred in his hadith was one of these sermons, or one like them that suggested a farewell.

Their words, “so give us your counsel”, mean a comprehensive and sufficient counsel. When they understood that he was bidding farewell, they asked him for counsel that would benefit them to hold fast to after him, and that would suffice whoever held fast to it and bring him happiness in this world and the Hereafter.
His words ﷺ, “I counsel you to fear Allah, and to listen and obey”: these two phrases bring together the happiness of this world and the Hereafter.
As for taqwā, it guarantees the happiness of the Hereafter to whoever holds fast to it. It is Allah's counsel to the first and the last, as the Exalted says:

“We have counselled those who were given the Book before you, and you, to fear Allah” [al-Nisāʾ 4:131]. An explanation of taqwā that suffices has already been given in the commentary on the hadith of the Prophet's counsel ﷺ to Muʿādh.

As for listening to and obeying those in authority over the Muslims, in it lies the happiness of this world. Through it the interests of the servants in their livelihood are kept in order, and through it they are helped to practise their religion openly and to obey their Lord,

as ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Nothing sets people right but a ruler, righteous or wicked. If he is wicked, the believer worships his Lord under him, and the wicked man is carried along in it until his appointed term.

Al-Ḥasan said of the rulers: They are in charge of five of our affairs: the Friday prayer, the congregation, the Eid, the frontiers and the prescribed punishments. By Allah, the religion is not kept upright except through them,
even if they are unjust and oppress. By Allah, what Allah sets right through them is more than what they corrupt; even though — by Allah — obeying them is galling, and parting from them is disbelief.

Al-Khallāl recorded in Kitāb al-Imārah, from the hadith of Abū Umāmah, who said: When they had prayed the night prayer, the Prophet ﷺ commanded his Companions: “Gather together, for I need you.” When he had finished the dawn prayer, he said: “Have you gathered as I commanded you?”
They said: Yes. He said: “Worship Allah and do not associate anything with Him. Have you understood this?”
— three times. We said: Yes. He said: “Keep up the prayer and give zakāh. Have you understood this?” — three times.
We said: Yes. He said: “Listen and obey” — three times — “Have you understood this?”
— three times. We said: Yes. The narrator said: We had thought that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would speak at length; then we considered his words, and he had gathered the whole matter for us.
The Prophet ﷺ also enjoined these two principles in his sermon at the Farewell Ḥajj, as Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded through the narration of Umm al-Ḥuṣayn al-Aḥmasiyyah, who said:

I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ preaching at the Farewell Ḥajj, and I heard him say: “O people, fear Allah; and even if a mutilated Abyssinian slave is put in command over you, listen to him and obey, so long as he establishes the Book of Allah among you.”
Muslim recorded from it the mention of listening and obeying.

Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī also recorded, from the hadith of Abū Umāmah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ preaching at the Farewell Ḥajj and saying: “Fear Allah, pray your five, fast your month,

pay the zakāh on your wealth and obey the one in charge of your affairs, and you will enter the Paradise of your Lord.” In another narration he said: “O people, there is no prophet after me and no nation after you,” and he related the hadith with the same meaning.

In the Musnad, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever meets Allah without associating anything with Him, having paid the zakāh on his wealth willingly and seeking the reward, and having listened and obeyed, will have Paradise” — or “will enter Paradise.”

His words ﷺ, “even if a slave is put in command over you” — and in one narration, “an Abyssinian” — come in a great many narrations from the Prophet ﷺ. It is one of the things the Prophet ﷺ was shown about the affairs of his nation after him,
including slaves coming to rule over them. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Listen and obey, even if an Abyssinian slave whose head is like a raisin is appointed over you.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: My dear friend ﷺ counselled me to listen and obey, even if it were an Abyssinian slave with mutilated limbs.
The hadiths with this meaning are very many.
This does not contradict his sayings ﷺ, “This matter will remain with Quraysh as long as two people remain,” “People follow Quraysh,” and “The imams are from Quraysh,”

because slaves may be given authority by a Qurashī ruler. This is supported by what al-Ḥākim recorded from the hadith of ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “The imams are from Quraysh: the righteous among them are rulers of the righteous,

and the wicked among them rulers of the wicked, and each has a right; so give everyone with a right his right. And if Quraysh put a mutilated Abyssinian slave in command over you, listen to him and obey.” Its chain is sound, but it has been narrated as mawqūf on ʿAlī (his own words), and al-Dāraquṭnī said: That is more likely.

It has been said that the Abyssinian slave is mentioned only by way of illustration, even if such a thing could not actually happen, as he said: “Whoever builds a mosque, even one like the nesting hollow of a sandgrouse…”
His words ﷺ: “Whoever of you lives after me will see much disagreement. So hold to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided, guided caliphs after me; bite onto it with your molar teeth.”
Here he ﷺ is foretelling what came to pass in his nation after him: much disagreement over the fundamentals of the religion and its branches, in statements, deeds and beliefs.
This agrees with what has been narrated from him about his nation splitting into seventy-odd sects, all of them in the Fire except one, namely those who follow what he and his Companions followed.

So too in this hadith he commanded that, in the face of division and disagreement, people hold fast to his Sunnah and to the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after him. The Sunnah is the path that is followed, so this includes holding fast to the beliefs, deeds and statements that he and his rightly guided caliphs held to.

This is the complete Sunnah. For this reason the Salaf of old applied the name Sunnah only to what includes all of that. Something to this effect has been narrated from al-Ḥasan, al-Awzāʿī and al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ.
Many of the later scholars restrict the name Sunnah to what concerns beliefs,

because they are the root of the religion, and whoever goes against them is in great danger. That these words come after the command to listen to and obey those in authority indicates that those in authority are to be obeyed only in obedience to Allah, as it is authentically reported that he said: “Obedience is only in what is right.”

In the Musnad, from Anas: Muʿādh ibn Jabal said: Messenger of Allah, tell me, if we have rulers over us who do not follow your Sunnah and do not take your command, what do you command concerning them?
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “There is no obedience to one who does not obey Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.”

Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “After me there will be put in charge of your affairs men who will extinguish some of the Sunnah, act by innovation and delay the prayer from its times.” I said: Messenger of Allah, if I live to see them, what shall I do?
He said: “There is no obedience to one who disobeys Allah.”

His command ﷺ to follow his Sunnah and the Sunnah of his rightly guided caliphs, after his command to listen to and obey those in authority in general, is evidence that the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs is to be followed as his Sunnah is followed, unlike that of other holders of authority.
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad and the Jāmiʿ of al-Tirmidhī, from Ḥudhayfah, who said: We were sitting with the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: “I do not know how long I shall remain among you;

so follow the example of the two after me” — and he pointed to Abū Bakr and ʿUmar — “hold to the counsel of ʿAmmār, and whatever Ibn Masʿūd tells you, believe him.” In another narration: “Hold to the counsel of Ibn Umm ʿAbd, and follow the guidance of ʿAmmār.”
So at the end of his life he ﷺ named explicitly those who were to be followed after him. The rightly guided caliphs whom he commanded us to follow are Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī,

for in the hadith of Safīnah, from the Prophet ﷺ: “The caliphate after me will be thirty years; then it will be kingship.” Imam Aḥmad declared it authentic and cited it as proof of the caliphate of the four imams.
Many of the imams stated explicitly that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was also a rightly guided caliph. This is indicated by what Imam Aḥmad recorded from the hadith of Ḥudhayfah,

from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Prophethood will be among you for as long as Allah wills it to be; then Allah will lift it when He wills to lift it. Then there will be a caliphate on the pattern of prophethood,

and it will be for as long as Allah wills it to be; then Allah will lift it when He wills to lift it. Then there will be a biting kingship for as long as Allah wills it to be; then He will lift it when He wills to lift it.

Then there will be a tyrannical kingship, and it will be for as long as Allah wills it to be; then He will lift it when He wills to lift it. Then there will be a caliphate on the pattern of prophethood.” Then he fell silent.
When ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz came to power, a man came to him and related this hadith to him, and he was delighted with it and pleased by it.
When Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn was sometimes asked about one of the drinks, he would say: An imam of guidance forbade it: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.
The scholars have differed over whether the agreement of the four caliphs counts as a consensus, or as a proof, when other Companions disagree with them.

There are two reported positions of Imam Aḥmad on it. In the time of al-Muʿtaḍid, Abū Khāzim the Ḥanafī ruled that the uterine kin (dhawū al-arḥām) inherit, and did not take into account those who differed from the caliphs; and his ruling to that effect was put into force throughout the lands.
If one of the four caliphs held a view, and none of them differed from him but some other Companion did, is his view given precedence over the other's view?

On this too the scholars hold two views. Aḥmad's explicit position is that his view is given precedence over that of the other Companions, and al-Khaṭṭābī and others said the same; the words of most of the Salaf indicate it,

especially in the case of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him), for it has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ by several routes that he said: “Allah has placed the truth on the tongue and the heart of ʿUmar.”
ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz used to follow his rulings, citing as evidence the Prophet's saying ﷺ: “Allah has placed the truth on the tongue and the heart of ʿUmar.”

Mālik said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and those in authority after him laid down practices (sunan); to take them is to hold fast to the Book of Allah and to gain strength in the religion of Allah. No one may replace them,

alter them, or consider anything that goes against them. Whoever is guided by them is guided, and whoever seeks help through them is helped; but whoever abandons them and follows other than the way of the believers, Allah will turn him over to what he has turned to and burn him in Hell — and evil is that destination.
ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam related from Mālik that he said: ʿUmar's resolve on that impressed me — meaning these words.
ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī reported these words from Mālik without relating them from ʿUmar.

Khalaf ibn Khalīfah said: I was present when ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, as caliph, was preaching to the people, and he said in his sermon: Whatever the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his two companions laid down is a fixed duty of religion; we take it, and we go no further than it.
Abū Nuʿaym reported, from the hadith of ʿArzab al-Kindī, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Things will arise after me, and the dearest of them to me is that you keep to what ʿUmar introduces.”
ʿAlī used to follow ʿUmar's rulings and judgements, and would say: ʿUmar was sound in judgement.
Ashʿath reported that al-Shaʿbī said: When people differ over something, look at how ʿUmar judged it, for he never judged a matter on which no judgement had been given before him without consulting.
Mujāhid said: When people differ over something, look at what ʿUmar did, and take it.

Ayyūb reported that al-Shaʿbī said: Look at what the nation of Muḥammad has agreed upon, for Allah would never make it agree upon misguidance; and when it differs, look at what ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb did, and take it.
ʿIkrimah was asked about the umm al-walad (a slave woman who has borne her master a child), and he said: She is freed by her master's death. He was asked: On what basis do you say that?
He said: On the basis of the Qurʾān. He was asked: Which part of the Qurʾān?
He said: “Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you” [al-Nisāʾ 4:59], and ʿUmar was one of those in authority.
Wakīʿ said: When ʿUmar and ʿAlī agree on something, that settles the matter.
It is narrated that Ibn Masʿūd used to swear by Allah that the straight path is the one on which ʿUmar stood firm until he entered Paradise.
In any case, whatever ʿUmar brought the Companions together on, so that they agreed on it in his time, is undoubtedly the truth, even if someone later differed over it:

such as his judgements on questions of inheritance like proportional reduction (ʿawl), and that in the cases of a husband with both parents, and a wife with both parents, the mother takes a third of the remainder; his judgement that one who has intercourse while in iḥrām continues with his rites and must make them up and offer a sacrificial animal;

what he decided concerning the wife of a missing man, in which the other caliphs also agreed with him; what he brought the people together on in the matter of the triple divorce and the prohibition of temporary marriage (mutʿah);

and what he did in establishing the register (dīwān), imposing the land tax (kharāj) on land taken by force, and making the pact of protection with the protected peoples (ahl al-dhimmah) on the conditions he set them, and so on.

The soundness of what ʿUmar brought the Companions together on, so that they agreed on it and no one differed in his time, is borne out by the Prophet's saying ﷺ: “I saw myself in a dream drawing water from a well. Then Abū Bakr came and drew a bucket or two, and there was weakness in his drawing,

and Allah will forgive him. Then Ibn al-Khaṭṭāb came, and it turned into a huge bucket (gharb), and I have never seen anyone do such wonderful work as his, until the people had drunk their fill and settled their camels by the water.” In one narration: “I have never seen a mighty man (ʿabqarī) among people draw as Ibn al-Khaṭṭāb drew”; and in another: “until he turned away with the trough overflowing.”

This indicates that ʿUmar did not die until he had put matters in their proper places and affairs had been set straight. That was because of the length of his rule, his giving his attention to new events and his concern with them. Abū Bakr's rule, by contrast, was short, and he was occupied in it with the conquests

and with sending out armies to fight, so that he had no time for many of the events that arose. Things may have happened in his time that did not reach him and were not brought to him, until those cases were brought to ʿUmar, who led people back to the truth in them and brought them to what was right.
As for what ʿUmar did not bring people together on, but on which he held a view of his own while allowing others to hold a view different from his,

such as the questions of the grandfather with the brothers and the question of divorce with the word “irrevocably” (al-battah), ʿUmar's view on it is not a proof binding the other Companions. And Allah knows best.
The caliphs were described as rightly guided (rāshidūn) only
because they knew the truth and judged by it. The rāshid is the opposite of the ghāwī (the errant), and the ghāwī is one who knows the truth and acts against it.

In one narration, “guided (mahdiyyīn)”: that is, Allah guides them to the truth and does not let them stray from it. So there are three categories: rāshid, ghāwī and ḍāll (astray). The rāshid knows the truth and follows it; the ghāwī knows it and does not follow it; and the ḍāll does not know it at all. So everyone rāshid is guided, and everyone fully guided is rāshid,
because guidance is only complete through knowing the truth and also acting on it.
His words, “bite onto it with your molar teeth,” are a figure for holding to it very firmly. The nawājidh are the molars.

His words, “And beware of newly invented matters, for every innovation is misguidance,” warn the nation against following newly invented and innovated matters, and he stressed this by saying, “every innovation is misguidance.”
What is meant by innovation is anything newly invented that has no basis in the Sharīʿah pointing to it. Whatever has a basis in the Sharīʿah pointing to it
is not an innovation in the Sharīʿah's sense, even if it is an innovation linguistically. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Jābir: the Prophet ﷺ used to say in his sermon:
“The best speech is the Book of Allah, the best guidance is the guidance of Muḥammad, the worst of matters are those newly invented, and every innovation is misguidance.”
Al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Kathīr ibn ʿAbdullāh al-Muzanī — and there is weakness in him — from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ,

who said: “Whoever introduces an innovation of misguidance which Allah and His Messenger are not pleased with bears the like of the sins of those who act on it, without that lessening their burdens in any way.”
Imam Aḥmad recorded, through the narration of Ghuḍayf ibn al-Ḥārith al-Thumālī, who said: ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān sent for me and said: We have brought the people together on two things:

raising the hands on the pulpits on Friday, and storytelling (qaṣaṣ) after the dawn and afternoon prayers. He said: These are, in my view, the best of your innovations, yet I will not answer you in any of them,
for the Prophet ﷺ said: “No people introduce an innovation but the like of it is taken away from the Sunnah.” So holding to a Sunnah is better than introducing an innovation.
Something similar has been narrated from Ibn ʿUmar as his own words.

His saying ﷺ, “every innovation is misguidance,” is one of the comprehensive words from which nothing is left out, and it is one of the great foundations of the religion. It resembles his saying: “Whoever introduces into this affair of ours what is not of it, it is rejected.”

So anything a person introduces and attributes to the religion, when it has no basis in the religion to go back to, is misguidance, and the religion is free of it; and this is so whether it concerns questions of belief, or of deeds, or of statements outward and inward.
As for the approval of certain innovations found in the words of the Salaf, that concerns only innovations in the linguistic sense, not in the Sharīʿah's sense.

An example is the saying of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) when he had gathered the people for the night prayer of Ramaḍān behind a single imam in the mosque, and then came out and saw them praying in this way: What an excellent innovation this is!
It is narrated that he said: If this is an innovation, what an excellent innovation it is.
It is narrated that Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said to him: This was not done before. ʿUmar said: I know; but it is good.

He meant that this act had not been done in this way before that time, but that it had bases in the Sharīʿah to go back to. One of them is that the Prophet ﷺ used to urge people to pray at night in Ramaḍān and encourage them to do it,
and in his time people would pray in the mosque in scattered groups and singly. He ﷺ led his Companions in prayer in Ramaḍān on more than one night,

and then refrained from doing so, giving as his reason that he feared it would be made obligatory for them and they would be unable to keep it up; and after him ﷺ there was no longer any fear of that.
It is narrated from him that he used to lead his Companions in prayer on the odd-numbered nights of the last ten.

Another is that he ﷺ commanded that the Sunnah of his rightly guided caliphs be followed, and this became part of the Sunnah of his rightly guided caliphs, for the people agreed on it in the time of ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī.

Another example is the first call to prayer on Friday. ʿUthmān added it because people needed it, ʿAlī confirmed it, and the Muslims have continued to practise it. It is narrated that Ibn ʿUmar said: It is an innovation; and perhaps he meant what his father meant about the night prayer of Ramaḍān.
Another is the compiling of the Qurʾān into a single volume. Zayd ibn Thābit hesitated over it and said to Abū Bakr and ʿUmar: How can you do what the Prophet ﷺ did not do?

Then he realised that it was in the general interest and agreed to compile it. The Prophet ﷺ used to command that the revelation be written down, and there is no difference between its being written in separate pieces or together; indeed, compiling it was better.

Likewise ʿUthmān's bringing the nation together on a single copy of the Qurʾān and destroying whatever differed from it, for fear that the nation would split. ʿAlī and most of the Companions approved of it, and it was the very essence of the general interest.
Likewise fighting those who refused to pay zakāh: ʿUmar and others hesitated over it until Abū Bakr showed ʿUmar its basis in the Sharīʿah, to which it goes back, and people agreed with him on it.

Another is storytelling (qaṣaṣ). We have already given Ghuḍayf ibn al-Ḥārith's saying that it is an innovation. Al-Ḥasan said: Storytelling is an innovation, and what an excellent innovation! How many a supplication answered, how many a need fulfilled, how many a brother gained!

By calling it an innovation, these men meant gathering for it at a fixed time; for the Prophet ﷺ had no fixed time at which he told stories to his Companions apart from his regular sermons on Fridays and at the Eids.

He only reminded them now and then, or when something happened that called for a reminder. Later the Companions agreed on fixing a time for it, as was mentioned above from Ibn Masʿūd, who used to remind his companions every Thursday.
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Speak to people once a week; if you must, then twice; and if you want more, then three times. And do not weary people.
In the Musnad, from ʿĀʾishah: she gave the storyteller of the people of Madīnah similar advice.
It is narrated that she said to ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr: Speak to people one day and leave them one day; do not weary them.
It is narrated that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ordered the storyteller to tell stories once every three days.
It is narrated that he said to him: Give the people a rest and do not burden them, and leave off storytelling on Saturday and Tuesday.
The ḥāfiẓ Abū Nuʿaym reported, with his chain of narration, from Ibrāhīm ibn al-Junayd: Ḥarmalah ibn Yaḥyā told us: I heard al-Shāfiʿī (Allah's mercy be upon him) say:
Innovation is of two kinds: praiseworthy innovation and blameworthy innovation. Whatever agrees with the Sunnah is praiseworthy, and whatever goes against the Sunnah is blameworthy.
And he cited as evidence ʿUmar's saying: What an excellent innovation it is!

What al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah have mercy on him) meant is what we mentioned earlier: that blameworthy innovation is that which has no basis in the Sharīʿah to go back to, and this is innovation as the Sharīʿah uses the term;

whereas praiseworthy innovation is what agrees with the Sunnah, meaning what has a basis in the Sunnah to go back to. It is an innovation only linguistically, not in the Sharīʿah's sense, because it agrees with the Sunnah.
Other words have been narrated from al-Shāfiʿī that explain this. He said: Newly invented matters are of two kinds. One is what is invented that goes against the Book, or the Sunnah,

or a report, or consensus; this is the innovation of misguidance. The other is what is invented of good, in which there is no opposition to any of these; this is a newly invented matter that is not blameworthy.
Many things have arisen that did not exist before, and the scholars have differed over whether they are a good innovation, going back to the Sunnah, or not.
One of them is the writing down of hadith. ʿUmar and a group of the Companions forbade it, while most permitted it, citing hadiths of the Sunnah as evidence for it.
Another is writing down commentary on the hadith and the Qurʾān. Some scholars disliked it, and many of them permitted it.

So too they have differed over writing down legal opinion (raʾy) on the lawful and the unlawful and the like, and over expanding discussion of transactions and of the deeds of the heart in ways not transmitted from the Companions and the Successors.
Imam Aḥmad disliked most of that.

In these times, now that the knowledge of the Salaf lies so far in the past, it is essential to record precisely all that has been transmitted from them in these matters, so that what knowledge existed in their time can be distinguished from what arose after them; by this the Sunnah is known from innovation.

It is authentically reported that Ibn Masʿūd said: Today you are upon the natural way (fiṭrah), but you will introduce new things, and new things will be introduced for you; so when you see a newly invented matter, hold to the first guidance.
Ibn Masʿūd said this in the time of the rightly guided caliphs.
Ibn Mahdī reported that Mālik said: None of these heresies (ahwāʾ) existed in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿUthmān.

By heresies Mālik seems to have meant the divisions that arose over the fundamentals of religion, such as the Khawārij, the Rāfiḍah, the Murjiʾah and the like, who held forth on declaring Muslims disbelievers and making their blood and wealth lawful,

or on their remaining in the Fire for ever, or on the elect of this nation being sinners; or the reverse of that, claiming that sins do not harm those who commit them, or that none of the people of tawḥīd will enter the Fire.
Graver than that is the talk that was introduced about Allah's acts, His decree and predestination, so that some denied them, claiming that by doing so they kept Allah free of injustice.
Graver still is the talk that was introduced about the essence and attributes of Allah, on which the Prophet ﷺ, his Companions and those who followed them in excellence were silent.
Some denied much of what has come in the Book and the Sunnah on this, claiming that they did so to declare Allah free of what reason requires Him to be declared free of,

and claiming that what this entails is impossible for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Others were not content to affirm it, but, along with affirming it, affirmed what is supposed to follow from it in the case of created beings. These entailments, whether denied or affirmed, are something the early generations of the nation kept silent about.

Among what was introduced into the nation after the age of the Companions and the Successors is speaking on the lawful and the unlawful by mere opinion, and rejecting much of what the Sunnah has brought on this because it goes against opinion and rational analogies.

Among what arose after that is speaking about the Reality (ḥaqīqah) by taste and unveiling, and claiming that the Reality is at odds with the Sharīʿah, that knowledge of Allah together with love suffices on its own, that there is no need for deeds, and that they are a veil;

or that only the common people need the Sharīʿah. Sometimes, added to that, there is talk about the essence and the attributes that is known with certainty to go against the Book, the Sunnah and the consensus of the Salaf of the nation. And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.
